findings.title: Hard-coded session signing key lets anyone forge a login as any user
findings.exposure_note: No account needed: the forged cookie replaces signing in.

cvss.rationale: AT:P because it needs a deployment that does not set SECRET_KEY, which the README does not mention; then full read/write of every account.

locations.note: falls back to a literal key committed to the repository (value redacted; fingerprint below)
trusts any correctly signed session cookie
the forged user_id becomes the acting user

path.summary: Anyone with the repository (or a leaked copy) knows the fallback key -> signs {"user_id": N} with Flask's session serializer -> login_required accepts it -> acts as user N on every route.
sanitisers_checked: SECRET_KEY from the environment: optional, with the literal as default
No server-side session store or session id to revoke
README and run.py do not set SECRET_KEY

preconditions: The app running locally: flask --app invoicer run --port 5057, with SECRET_KEY unset (as in the README).
Read the fallback key at invoicer/__init__.py:11 (not reproduced here).
steps: GET /invoices without a cookie: 401.
Sign {'user_id': 2} with the fallback key using Flask's SecureCookieSessionInterface().get_signing_serializer (the PoC file shows the one-liner) and export it as FORGED_SESSION.
GET /invoices with Cookie: session=$FORGED_SESSION.

safe_payload.payload: A session cookie for user_id 2 (bob), signed with the fallback key; read-only GET.
safe_payload.proof: The response lists bob's invoices (INV-2002) without any login.

repro.expected_secure: The app refuses to start without SECRET_KEY, so no known key ever signs sessions; the forged cookie is rejected (401).
repro.actual_vulnerable: 200 with bob's invoices INV-2001 and INV-2002.

findings.impact: Complete authentication bypass on any deployment that forgot SECRET_KEY: read, create and import invoices as any user. Every "authenticated" finding below (F-4 to F-8, F-10, F-13) becomes reachable without an account.

fix.change: Remove the fallback: read SECRET_KEY from the environment and raise at start-up when it is missing. Rotate the key on any deployment that used the fallback (all sessions are invalidated).
fix.safer_api: app.config["SECRET_KEY"] = os.environ["SECRET_KEY"] (or a secrets manager); generate keys with secrets.token_hex(32).

findings.title: pull_request_target workflow checks out and runs untrusted pull-request code with a write token
findings.owasp: A08:2025 Software or Data Integrity Failures
findings.exposure_note: Any GitHub user who can open a pull request.

cvss.rationale: Code execution in the privileged job (VC/VI:H); the pull-requests: write token and persisted checkout credentials reach the repository (SI:H).

locations.note: runs in the base repository context, with secrets and a write token
checks out the PR author's code
installs the PR's requirements (arbitrary packages)
runs the PR's conftest.py and tests

path.summary: Fork PR opened -> pull_request_target job starts with GITHUB_TOKEN (pull-requests: write) -> checkout of head.sha with persisted credentials -> pip install / pytest execute PR-controlled code in that job.
sanitisers_checked: permissions limited to contents: read, pull-requests: write

preconditions: The repository accepts pull requests from forks (any public repository does).
steps: From a fork, add a conftest.py that prints a marker, e.g. print("CANARY-7f2") (and nothing else).
Open a pull request against the default branch.
Open the run of the ci workflow for that PR and look for the marker in the "pytest -q" step log.

safe_payload.proof: The marker appears in the privileged workflow run triggered by pull_request_target.

repro.expected_secure: Untrusted PR code only runs in a pull_request workflow with a read-only token and no secrets.
repro.actual_vulnerable: PR code runs inside the pull_request_target job, which holds a pull-requests: write token.

poc.reason: Needs a GitHub repository and a fork PR; verification here was limited to the local app. Traced from the workflow file.

findings.impact: A stranger can run code in CI with a token that can write to pull requests (and, through the persisted checkout credentials, whatever contents: allows), poison caches used by later trusted runs, and read any secrets added to this workflow later.

fix.change: Run tests on pull_request (no secrets, read-only token). If a comment is needed, post it from a separate workflow_run workflow that never checks out or executes PR code. Set persist-credentials: false on checkout.
fix.safer_api: on: pull_request; a follow-up on: workflow_run job for commenting; permissions: contents: read.

regression_test.note: A workflow change, not code: guard it by running zizmor (or the Semgrep rule pull-request-target-code-checkout) in CI.

findings.title: Pull-request title is expanded into a shell script in the privileged workflow
findings.exposure_note: Any GitHub user who can open a pull request.

cvss.rationale: Same privileged job as F-2; the title alone is enough, with no code in the PR.

locations.note: the expression is substituted into the script before bash parses it

path.summary: PR title (attacker-controlled) -> ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }} substituted into the run: script text -> bash executes it in the pull_request_target job.
sanitisers_checked: Quoting in the script does not help: the substitution happens before the shell parses

preconditions: The repository accepts pull requests from forks (any public repository does).
steps: Open a pull request whose title is: x" && echo "CANARY-3c1
Read the "Summarise" step log of the ci workflow run.

safe_payload.proof: The log shows CANARY-3c1 on its own line, printed by the injected echo.

repro.expected_secure: The title is printed literally, quotes and all.
repro.actual_vulnerable: The title closes the string and runs a second command.

poc.reason: Needs a GitHub repository; traced from the workflow file.

findings.impact: Same as F-2, but needs no code change: a crafted PR title runs commands in the privileged job. Fixing F-2 alone does not fix this.

fix.change: Pass the value through the environment: env: TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}, then run: echo "Tests passed for $TITLE".
fix.safer_api: env: indirection for every github.event.* value used in run: scripts.

findings.title: Report title is compiled as a Jinja template (server-side template injection)

cvss.rationale: Jinja expressions in an unsandboxed environment lead to code execution as the app user.

locations.note: input concatenated into template source

path.summary: GET /invoices/report?title=... -> concatenated into the template text -> render_template_string compiles and evaluates it.
sanitisers_checked: Auto-escaping only escapes variables, not template source

preconditions: The app running locally: flask --app invoicer run --port 5057, with SECRET_KEY unset (as in the README).
POST /login with email=alice@example.test&password=alice-test-pw (seeded test account); keep the session cookie.
steps: GET /invoices/report?title={{7*191}}

safe_payload.proof: The page heading reads 1337, a value the server computed; the request never contains it.

findings.impact: Any signed-in user (or anyone, via F-1) can evaluate Jinja expressions on the server, which in an unsandboxed environment reaches Python objects and runs code as the app user: database, uploaded files, environment secrets.

fix.change:
Render a fixed template and pass the title as a variable: render_template_string("

{{ title }}

...", title=title, rows=rows), or move it to a template file.

findings.title: SQL injection in invoice search returns other users' invoices

cvss.rationale: sqlite3 execute() runs one statement, so reads (UNION/boolean) but no stacked writes.

locations.note: f-string builds the SQL text

path.summary: GET /invoices/search?q=... -> interpolated into the f-string SQL -> sqlite3 execute.
sanitisers_checked: g.user_id is also interpolated, but comes from the session
sqlite3 rejects stacked statements (limits impact to reads)

preconditions: The app running locally: flask --app invoicer run --port 5057, with SECRET_KEY unset (as in the README).
POST /login with email=alice@example.test&password=alice-test-pw (seeded test account); keep the session cookie.
steps: GET /invoices/search?q=' OR 1=1 --
GET /invoices/search?q=' OR 1=2 --

safe_payload.proof: INV-2001 (bob's) is returned only for the true condition.

repro.expected_secure: Both return an empty list (no customer contains the text).
repro.actual_vulnerable: The true condition returns all four invoices, including bob's INV-2001 and INV-2002.

findings.impact: Any signed-in user can read every invoice, and with UNION SELECT the users table (emails and password hashes).

fix.change: Bind both values: execute(f"SELECT {COLUMNS} FROM invoices WHERE owner_id = ? AND customer LIKE ?", (g.user_id, f"%{q}%")).
fix.safer_api: sqlite3 parameters (?), or SQLAlchemy Core/ORM expressions.

findings.title: Blind SQL injection through the invoice list sort parameter

cvss.rationale: Boolean-blind reads of any table, one bit per request.

locations.note: identifier position: parameters cannot be used here, so it needs an allow-list

path.summary: GET /invoices?sort=... -> interpolated after ORDER BY -> sqlite3 execute; the condition inside CASE decides the row order.
sanitisers_checked: owner_id is bound (?), so rows stay alice's, but the expression can read other tables in subqueries

preconditions: The app running locally: flask --app invoicer run --port 5057, with SECRET_KEY unset (as in the README).
POST /login with email=alice@example.test&password=alice-test-pw (seeded test account); keep the session cookie.
steps: GET /invoices?sort=CASE WHEN (1=1) THEN amount ELSE number END
GET /invoices?sort=CASE WHEN (1=2) THEN amount ELSE number END

safe_payload.payload: CASE WHEN (1=1) THEN amount ELSE number END (and 1=2)
safe_payload.proof: The true condition sorts by amount (INV-1002, 450.5, first); the false one by number.

repro.expected_secure: 400 for anything but a known column.
repro.actual_vulnerable: The order follows the injected condition.

findings.impact: Replacing 1=1 with a subquery condition (e.g. on users.password_hash) leaks any value bit by bit to a signed-in user.

fix.change: Allow-list the column: SORTABLE = {"number", "customer", "amount", "status"}; abort(400) for anything else.
fix.safer_api: A dict from public sort names to column names.

findings.title: Path traversal in attachment downloads reads any file the app can read

cvss.rationale: Read-only, any file readable by the process.

locations.note: ../ is kept; an absolute name replaces the base

path.summary: GET /attachments?name=../x -> os.path.join keeps ../ (and an absolute name discards UPLOAD_DIR) -> isfile -> send_file.

preconditions: The app running locally: flask --app invoicer run --port 5057, with SECRET_KEY unset (as in the README).

findings.title: Invoice import parses YAML with the unsafe loader (code execution)
findings.owasp: A08:2025 Software or Data Integrity Failures

cvss.rationale: yaml.Loader constructs arbitrary Python objects, including callables.

path.summary: POST /invoices/import (multipart file) -> yaml.load with yaml.Loader -> python/object/apply tags call arbitrary functions.
sanitisers_checked: Loader=yaml.Loader is the unsafe loader in every PyYAML version

preconditions: The app running locally: flask --app invoicer run --port 5057, with SECRET_KEY unset (as in the README).
POST /login with email=alice@example.test&password=alice-test-pw (seeded test account); keep the session cookie.
steps: Upload a YAML list whose number field uses a Python tag that calls a harmless builtin, in-process, as the regression test does.

safe_payload.payload: None sent to the running app: a proof needs a tag that calls a function, which the PoC safety rules forbid. The regression test uses builtins.str in-process instead.
safe_payload.proof: In the test, the import returns 201 and stores a value built by calling str(), showing tags are honoured.

poc.reason: Proving it against a running app needs a payload that calls a function, which the safety rules forbid. The in-process regression test shows the loader honours Python tags (201 instead of 400).

findings.impact: Any signed-in user (anyone, with F-1) can run code on the server by uploading a crafted YAML file, and can also do it via CSRF (F-17).

fix.change: yaml.safe_load, catch yaml.YAMLError (400), and check the result is a list of dicts with the expected keys.
fix.safer_api: yaml.safe_load, or JSON with a schema.

regression_test.name: test_import_rejects_python_yaml_tags
regression_test.sketch:
def test_import_rejects_python_yaml_tags(client, login):
    login(*ALICE)
    doc = b"- number: !!python/object/apply:builtins.str [INV-9001]\n  customer: Canary\n  amount: 1\n"
    resp = client.post("/invoices/import", data={"file": (io.BytesIO(doc), "x.yaml")},
                       content_type="multipart/form-data")
    assert resp.status_code == 400

The test sends a Python tag that only calls str(), in-process on the test client, never to a running server.

findings.title: Password reset tokens are short, non-cryptographic and never expire

cvss.rationale: Predicting the Mersenne Twister state needs many observed tokens (an account of the attacker's own, PR:L) and is hard from truncated outputs (AC:H).

locations.snippet: db.execute("UPDATE users SET reset_token = ? WHERE email = ?", (token, email))
locations.note: stored with no expiry
no attempt limit

path.summary: POST /password-reset -> 8 characters from random (Mersenne Twister) -> stored without expiry -> POST /password-reset/confirm accepts it with unlimited attempts.
sanitisers_checked: about 47.6 bits of space; no expiry; no attempt limit
path.gap: Not shown: recovering the generator state from observed tokens. random.choices maps each 53-bit float to one of 62 characters, so known state-recovery attacks need many tokens and are not demonstrated here.

preconditions: The app running locally: flask --app invoicer run --port 5057, with SECRET_KEY unset (as in the README).
An account of the attacker's own, to receive reset tokens.
steps: Request resets for your own account repeatedly and record the tokens.
Use them to model the generator, then request a reset for the victim and predict the token.

safe_payload.payload: None sent: prediction was not attempted.
safe_payload.proof: The regression test shows the token is 8 characters (expected at least 32).

repro.expected_secure: A 256-bit secrets.token_urlsafe token that expires in minutes and is single use.
repro.actual_vulnerable: An 8-character random.choices token with no expiry.

poc.reason: Token prediction is not a canary-safe action and was not attempted.

findings.impact: If the token can be predicted (or brute-forced, given unlimited attempts and no expiry), an attacker takes over any account by email address.

fix.change: token = secrets.token_urlsafe(32); store a hash of it with an expiry (15 minutes); delete it on use; compare with hmac.compare_digest; rate-limit confirm attempts.

regression_test.name: test_reset_token_is_long_enough
regression_test.sketch:
def test_reset_token_is_long_enough(client):

    with client.application.app_context():
        token = get_db().execute("SELECT reset_token FROM users WHERE id = 1").fetchone()[0]
    assert len(token) >= 32

locations.note: checks the scheme only

path.summary: POST /webhooks/test {"url": ...} -> scheme check only -> requests.get (follows redirects) -> first 500 characters returned.
sanitisers_checked: Scheme check (http/https) does not restrict hosts

preconditions: The app running locally: flask --app invoicer run --port 5057, with SECRET_KEY unset (as in the README).
POST /login with email=alice@example.test&password=alice-test-pw (seeded test account); keep the session cookie.
steps: POST /webhooks/test with {"url": "http://127.0.0.1:5057/healthz"}

safe_payload.proof: The response body contains invoicer-ok, fetched by the server from a loopback-only URL.

repro.expected_secure: 400 for loopback, private and link-local destinations.

findings.impact: Reads services only the server can reach: admin ports, internal APIs and, in the cloud, the instance metadata service and its credentials (not tested: metadata addresses are never targeted).

fix.change: Resolve the host and reject non-global addresses (ipaddress.ip_address(a).is_global for every resolved address); disable redirects; do not return the body.
fix.safer_api: An egress allow-list or proxy for webhook delivery.

def test_webhook_test_refuses_loopback_urls(client, login, monkeypatch):
    calls = []
    monkeypatch.setattr(
        "invoicer.webhooks.requests.get",
        lambda url, **kw: calls.append(url) or SimpleNamespace(status_code=200, text="ok"),
    )
    login(*ALICE)
    resp = client.post("/webhooks/test", json={"url": "http://127.0.0.1/healthz"})
    assert resp.status_code == 400 and calls == []

findings.title: GitHub Actions pinned to mutable tags, including a third-party action that receives the token
findings.exposure_note: Needs control of the action's repository (a compromised maintainer or tag).

cvss.rationale: Requires an upstream compromise (AC:H, AT:P); then code runs with the token.

locations.note: third-party; receives GITHUB_TOKEN (line 27)

path.summary: A moved v2 tag on the third-party action -> the next workflow run executes the new code with GITHUB_TOKEN (pull-requests: write).

preconditions: Control of the thollander/actions-comment-pull-request repository or its v2 tag.
steps: Not reproducible without compromising a third party; traced from the workflow file.

safe_payload.proof: The uses: lines reference tags, not commit SHAs.

findings.impact: If the action or its tag is compromised (as happened to tj-actions/changed-files in 2025), its new code runs with this workflow's token.

fix.change: Pin every action to a full commit SHA with the version in a comment, and let Dependabot (package-ecosystem: github-actions) update them.

findings.title: requests 2.31.0 can leak .netrc credentials to a host chosen through the SSRF endpoint (CVE-2024-47081)
findings.exposure_note: Only matters on a server with a .netrc file.

cvss.rationale: AT:P: needs a .netrc on the server; the credentials belong to other systems (SC:H).

locations.note: fixed in 2.32.4
attacker-chosen URL with default trust_env=True

path.summary: Attacker-chosen URL (F-13) -> requests.get with trust_env -> a crafted URL makes requests send .netrc credentials for another host.
sanitisers_checked: trust_env is left at its default (True)
Whether servers have a .netrc is unknown

preconditions: A server with a .netrc file.
steps: Not run: it needs a .netrc on the target and an external receiving host; the URL parsing issue is described in GHSA-9hjg-9r4m-mvj7.

safe_payload.proof: Reachability: requests.get with a request-supplied URL at webhooks.py:15.

poc.reason: Needs an external host to receive the credentials, which the safety rules forbid.

findings.impact: Credentials stored in the server's .netrc (package registries, internal services) can be sent to the attacker's host.

fix.change: Upgrade requests to 2.33.0 or later (also fixes DEP-008 and DEP-009); fixing F-13 removes the attacker-chosen URL.
fix.safer_api: A requests.Session with trust_env=False for outbound webhook calls.

findings.title: run.py starts the Werkzeug debugger on all interfaces
findings.exposure_note: Anyone on the same network as a developer who runs python run.py.

cvss.rationale: Adjacent network (a developer machine); the debugger console is PIN-protected (AC:H) but the PIN is derivable with file reads such as F-8.

path.summary: python run.py -> Werkzeug dev server with the interactive debugger, bound to 0.0.0.0 -> any error page offers a Python console after the PIN.
sanitisers_checked: Debugger PIN (derivable from machine id, MAC and paths)
The README starts the app with flask run, without debug, so production use of run.py is not shown

preconditions: A developer runs python run.py on a shared network.
steps: From another machine, open http://<developer-ip>:5000/console.

safe_payload.proof: The Werkzeug debugger PIN prompt is served to a remote address.

repro.expected_secure: Debug off unless FLASK_DEBUG is set, and bound to 127.0.0.1.

poc.reason: The verification target was started with flask run (no debugger), as the README says; run.py was not started.

findings.impact: Code execution on a developer machine for someone on the same network, if they get the PIN (made easier by F-8 file reads, and by CVE-2024-34069 in Werkzeug 3.0.1).

fix.change: app.run(host="127.0.0.1", debug=os.environ.get("FLASK_DEBUG") == "1"), or delete run.py and use flask run.
fix.safer_api: flask --app invoicer run (debug off by default).

findings.title: No CSRF protection on cookie-authenticated form posts (including the YAML import)
findings.exposure_note: Any website a signed-in user visits.

cvss.rationale: Rated for the direct effect (invoices created, sign-out). AT:P because browsers that default cookies to SameSite=Lax block it; the chain to F-10 is rated there.

locations.note: multipart form post, no token
no CSRF extension and no SameSite setting

path.summary: Attacker page auto-submits a multipart form to /invoices/import -> the browser attaches the session cookie (where SameSite is not enforced) -> import runs as the victim.
sanitisers_checked: Chromium defaults unspecified SameSite to Lax; Safari and Firefox defaults differ

preconditions: The app running locally: flask --app invoicer run --port 5057, with SECRET_KEY unset (as in the README).
A victim signed in, using a browser that does not default to SameSite=Lax.
steps: Host a page that auto-submits a multipart form with a harmless one-invoice YAML file to http://127.0.0.1:5057/invoices/import.
Have the victim open it.

safe_payload.payload: A one-row YAML file with customer CANARY-CSRF
safe_payload.proof: A draft invoice for CANARY-CSRF appears in the victim's list.

poc.reason: Needs a browser and a second origin; run_poc sends requests directly and cannot show cross-site cookie behaviour.

findings.impact: A malicious page can act as a signed-in victim: import invoices, sign them out and, combined with F-10, run code on the server through their session.

fix.change: Add CSRFProtect (Flask-WTF) for form posts and set SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE="Lax" and SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=True.

findings.title: Sign-in logs the submitted password
findings.owasp: A09:2025 Security Logging and Alerting Failures
findings.exposure_note: Readable by whoever can read the logs.

cvss.rationale: AT:P: only written when the invoicer.auth logger is at INFO (the root default is WARNING); then every password, including wrong ones, is in plain text.

locations.snippet: log.info("login attempt email=%s password=%s", email, password)

path.summary: POST /login -> password read from the form -> log.info writes it before it is checked.
sanitisers_checked: Logger level not configured in the repository (INFO in many deployments)

preconditions: Logging at INFO for invoicer.auth.
steps: Sign in (with any password) and read the application log.

safe_payload.payload: A normal login with the test account
safe_payload.proof: The regression test captures the log line containing the password.

poc.reason: The local instance logs at WARNING, so nothing is written; shown in-process by the regression test with INFO capture.

findings.impact: Anyone with log access (operators, log pipelines, a log-reading bug) gets users' passwords, which are often reused elsewhere.

fix.change: Log the attempt without the password: log.info("login attempt email=%s", email). Add a redacting logging.Filter as a backstop.
fix.safer_api: Structured logging with an allow-list of fields.

regression_test.name: test_login_does_not_log_the_password
regression_test.sketch:
def test_login_does_not_log_the_password(client, caplog):
    caplog.set_level("INFO")
    client.post("/login", data={"email": ALICE[0], "password": ALICE[1]})
    assert ALICE[1] not in caplog.text
regression_test.note: Fails on the vulnerable code (regression/vulnerable_run.txt: 11 failed) and passes with the recommended fix applied (regression/fixed_run.txt: 13 passed, including the existing tests).

variant_rules.rule:
rules:
  - id: sql-text-from-request
    message: >-
      SQL text is built from request data. Pass values as bound parameters, and take
      identifiers (ORDER BY columns) from an allow-list.
    severity: ERROR
    languages: [python]
    metadata:
      cwe: "CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command"
      written_for: invoicer security audit (variant analysis of F-2)
    mode: taint
    pattern-sources:
      - pattern: flask.request.$PART.get(...)
      - pattern: flask.request.$PART[...]
    pattern-sinks:
      - patterns:
          - pattern: $DB.execute($QUERY, ...)
          - focus-metavariable: $QUERY
    pattern-sanitizers:
      - pattern: int(...)
      - patterns:  # an allow-list check that rejects anything else
          - pattern-inside: |
              if $V not in $ALLOWED:
                  ...
              ...
          - pattern: $V
variant_rules.test_note: Run with Semgrep 1.184.0: matches invoices.py:20 (F-6) and :30 (F-5) and nothing else, including not the COLUMNS-only queries at :38 and :48; no matches on the fixed copy (allow-listed sort, bound LIKE).

variant_rules.rule:
rules:
  - id: template-text-from-request
    message: >-
      Template source is built from request data, so Jinja evaluates it (SSTI). Render a fixed
      template and pass the value as a variable.
    severity: ERROR
    languages: [python]
    metadata:
      cwe: "CWE-1336: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements Used in a Template Engine"
      written_for: invoicer security audit (variant analysis of F-1)
    mode: taint
    pattern-sources:
      - pattern: flask.request.$PART.get(...)
      - pattern: flask.request.$PART[...]
    pattern-sinks:
      - patterns:
          - pattern-either:
              - pattern: flask.render_template_string($SRC, ...)
              - pattern: jinja2.Template($SRC, ...)
              - pattern: $ENV.from_string($SRC, ...)
          - focus-metavariable: $SRC
variant_rules.test_note: Run with Semgrep 1.184.0: matches invoices.py:50 (F-4) only; no matches on the fixed copy.

observations.title: No rate limiting or lockout on sign-in and reset confirmation
observations.note: Unlimited password guesses and reset-token guesses (makes F-11 worse). Add per-account and per-IP limits (e.g. Flask-Limiter).

observations.title: Reset token compared with != rather than in constant time
observations.note: Low practical impact over a network; use hmac.compare_digest when fixing F-11.

observations.title: Session cookie flags left at Flask defaults
observations.note: SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE is False and SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE unset. Set Secure and SameSite=Lax (also mitigates F-17). The edge proxy may set these; not visible in the repository.

not_reviewed.reason: gitleaks is not installed and the example is not its own git repository, so history was not scanned; the key in F-1 has in_git_history unknown.
No Dockerfile, IaC or proxy configuration in the repository; TLS, request size limits and cookie flags set at the edge are unknown.
osv-scanner and Trivy are not installed; pip-audit resolved requirements.txt only.

limitations: gitleaks, osv-scanner and Trivy were not installed (not_run): secrets were scanned in the working tree only with scan_secrets.py, and dependencies only through pip-audit.
Verification ran against a local instance with seeded test accounts; behaviour behind a real proxy (size limits, cookie flags) may differ.

F-10, F-11, F-12 and F-15 were not confirmed: proving them would need a code-execution payload, token prediction, a denial-of-service payload or an external receiving host, all forbidden by the safety rules.
The CI findings (F-2, F-3, F-14) are traced from the workflow file; they were not exercised on GitHub.
CVSS vectors use base metrics only; no threat or environmental metrics.
Recon found routes by pattern; all six modules were read to confirm there are no others.

summary.headline: 18 findings in Invoicer: 3 P0 (session forgery with the hard-coded key, and two ways for a pull request to run code in the privileged CI job), 9 P1. 8 findings confirmed against a local instance with canary PoCs. Not covered: git history and dependencies beyond requirements.txt.
